rows.question: When is a vulnerability in GitLab's code considered fixed?
rows.answer: A vulnerability in GitLab’s code is considered fixed when the vulnerability has been addressed, validated as no longer present, and a version of the code containing the fix has been made available in packaged form to GitLab users and self-hosting users [1]. This includes making fixes available to GitLab team members responsible for deploying GitLab to hosted or managed installations [1]. A vulnerability is not considered fixed until a version containing the fix is shipped and accessible to users [1]. However, a vulnerability in code is also considered fixed before deployment as long as the updated packages or images have been made available to the intended consumers of those packages [1]. In managed or hosted environments for which GitLab is responsible, deployment of the remediated code via packages or images must be performed before the vulnerability is considered fixed in those environments [1].
rows.judge_reason: It states that the vulnerability is fixed once a version containing the fix is packaged and available to users, not necessarily deployed, with the exception of GitLab-managed environments.

rows.question: Can on-call engineers recover after a demanding shift?
rows.answer:

Engineers should also communicate with their manager about the pressures of the shift so alerts, processes, or incident resolution can be improved [2].

Time in lieu must be taken within 2 weeks of shift completion and requested through Workday by selecting “Time Off in Lieu” [1]. rows.question: A fast-quarantined test is still broken after 3 days. What are the options, and when would it be deleted?
rows.answer:
If a fast-quarantined test is still broken after 3 days, the options are to implement a fix, remove the test entirely if it duplicates other tests or the flakiness cannot be fixed, or convert it to long-term quarantine with an updated timeline [1]. If you cannot meet the 3-day timeline, you must always convert to long-term quarantine [1]. Fast quarantine has a maximum of 3 days, and the required action is to fix, remove, or convert to long-term [3].

For deletion: long-term quarantine has a maximum duration of 3 months [4]. There is a 1-week deletion warning, and automatic deletion occurs after 3 months, permanently removing the test [3]. The owner or Engineering Manager is alerted that the test is to be deleted, and the Quarantine Cleanup System creates a deletion merge request to be actioned by the owning team within a week [4]. If ownership is not maintained, the test is automatically deleted after 3 months [2].
rows.judge_reason: It states the options (fix, remove, or convert to long-term quarantine) and correctly notes that long-term quarantine lasts at most 3 months before automatic deletion, with only extra non-contradictory detail.

rows.question: I review merge requests and I'm going on vacation. What should I do with my reviews?

The person checking does not have to do the reviews themselves; they can assign the merge requests to themselves for review or use Reviewer Roulette to find other Technical Writers to review [2].

More generally, if you are assigned as a Reviewer and cannot review because you are out of working hours, lack understanding, or do not have capacity, you should mention this to the merge request author so they can find another maintainer or an alternate team member [1]. For Distribution, if you are assigned directly as a Reviewer, use your judgment, and if you will not be able to work on it soon, try to find another Reviewer [5]. After completing a review, keep yourself as a reviewer and submit the review with a summary comment and the appropriate review status [6].

rows.question: Do support engineers get Family and Friends days off like everyone else?
rows.answer: Yes—at least for FY26, Support Team members can take Family and Friends days: Support continues to operate as normal during Family and Friends Days, and in FY26 team members are free to take off a total of 4 days at their convenience to celebrate and record as a Family and Friends day, following the same guidelines as Choosing and Recording Time Off [1]. More broadly, Family & Friends days are maintained as a team member benefit with different iterations each fiscal year, and team members are strongly encouraged to take the day off if their role allows it [2]. The Support Team follows GitLab’s paid time off policy while balancing the need to deliver customer support every day [3].
rows.judge_reason: It states Support operates normally on Family and Friends Days and that FY26 Support members may take 4 days at their convenience, matching the expected key facts.

rows.question: I want to run a raffle at our conference booth. Are there limits on the prizes?
rows.answer: The sources do not use the word “raffle”; they address conference sweepstakes. Under GitLab’s conference sweepstakes process, the only type of promotional game permitted is a sweepstakes [4]. For a conference sweepstakes, each individual prize must be less than $600 USD [4], and the total aggregate value of all prizes must be less than $1,000 USD [4]; the source references exceptions but does not include their details [4]. Cash and cash equivalents, including gift cards, are not permitted as prizes or incentives [5]. There is also a limit of one prize per entrant, family, or household [3], and winners may not substitute or transfer a prize [3]. Country-specific limits apply, including Denmark (individual prize less than $30 USD), New Zealand (aggregate less than $500 USD), the Netherlands (aggregate less than $500 USD and full abbreviated rules in advertisements), and Australia (conditions including no prize substitution) [4]. Sweepstakes must also comply with GitLab’s standard approval processes and applicable laws [5].
rows.judge_reason: The system gives the key standard-process limits—individual prizes under $600 USD and aggregate prizes under $1,000 USD—and adds extra details without contradicting the expected answer.
